axes.label: Economy & Cost of Living
axes.description: Measures preferences on state intervention vs market deregulation, price controls, wage policies, and subsidy regimes.

axes.label: Security
axes.description: Measures approaches to internal security, policing models (state vs federal), operational leadership, and negotiation strategies.

axes.label: Power Rotation & Restructuring
axes.description: Measures positions on geopolitical power rotation, structural devolution of powers, and constitutional electoral reforms.

axes.label: Education & Human Capital
axes.description: Measures views on state vs federal responsibility, basic education declarations, public university tuition funding, and vocational priorities.

axes.label: Governance & Anti-Corruption
axes.description: Measures strategies for anti-corruption enforcement, institutional autonomy, revenue management, and central vs local accountability.

scoringRules.axisWeighting: user-ranked via drag-and-drop; weights normalised to sum to 1

decisionLog: Q1: Market reform/deregulation scored +2 (q1b); subsidy restoration scored -2 (q1a); targeted intervention/price capping scored -1 (q1c); direct social transfer scored +1 (q1d).

Q2: Radical statutory wage mandate (₦500k) scored -2 (q2a); direct social welfare transfer scored -1 (q2d); productivity-tied wage growth scored +1 (q2b); fully decentralised/market wage setting scored +2 (q2c).

Q3: Pure macro stability & investor confidence scored +2 (q3a); immediate price intervention/relief scored -2 (q3b); structural diversification/production expansion scored -1 (q3c); fiscal discipline/anti-corruption primacy scored +1 (q3d).

Q4: Direct executive intervention scored -2 (q4a); state policing devolution scored +2 (q4b); structural security architecture overhaul scored +1 (q4c); socio-economic root cause approach scored -1 (q4d).
Q5: Executive leadership focus scored -2 (q5a); state policing decentralisation scored +2 (q5b); socio-economic poverty focus scored -1 (q5c); ethno-religious cohesion focus scored +1 (q5d).
Q6: Kinetic elimination scored +2 (q6b); local amnesty/reconciliation scored +1 (q6c); pragmatic negotiation scored -1 (q6a); non-kinetic socio-economic prevention scored -2 (q6d).
Q7: Unconditional geopolitical rotation scored -2 (q7a); conditional rotation scored -1 (q7c); structural devolution to regions scored +1 (q7d); pure meritocracy/anti-rotation scored +2 (q7b).

Q8: Full regional/state restructuring scored +2 (q8a); targeted security/local autonomy scored +1 (q8c); electoral threshold reform scored -1 (q8b); constitutional universal free education scored -2 (q8d).

Q9: State of emergency / universal free education scored -2 (q9a); vocational/market alignment scored -1 (q9d); performance target investments scored +1 (q9b); full state decentralisation scored +2 (q9c).

Q10: Universal free university scored -2 (q10a); targeted STEM/education subsidy scored -1 (q10c); basic education priority / fiscal realism scored +1 (q10d); user-paid with student loan access scored +2 (q10b).

Q11: Direct presidential anti-corruption crusade scored -2 (q11a); decentralised local accountability scored -1 (q11d); restitution priority scored +1 (q11c); institutional independence/autonomy scored +2 (q11b).

Q12: Universal fuel subsidy restoration scored -2 (q12d); excess revenue direct welfare transfers scored -1 (q12a); sovereign wealth fund savings scored +1 (q12b); full market deregulation & subsidy removal scored +2 (q12c).

questions.prompt: A bag of rice that cost ₦30,000 two years ago now costs ₦80,000. What should the government do first?

options.text: Restore a form of fuel subsidy and reopen land borders to bring down transport and food costs fast.
Keep the reforms in place and let the market stabilise — reversing now would waste the pain already endured.
Declare an emergency on food production and cap essential prices while investing in agriculture.
Channel excess crude oil revenue directly into cash transfers and welfare for the poorest Nigerians.

questions.prompt: Nigeria's minimum wage is ₦70,000. What is the right approach?

options.text: Raise it immediately to a living wage (₦500,000) and provide 24-hour electricity to reduce business costs.
Phase in wage increases tied to productivity and revenue, without destabilising small businesses.
Leave wage setting to states and the private sector; the federal government should focus on inflation.
Prioritise cash transfers over wage hikes — direct payments reach the informal sector that wages miss.

questions.prompt: The naira has stabilised but prices remain high. What matters more?

options.text: Macroeconomic stability — a strong naira and investor confidence will eventually trickle down.
The price of bread today — macro numbers mean nothing if people cannot eat.
Breaking dependence on oil and building productive capacity so the economy is not hostage to crude prices.
Fiscal discipline and anti-corruption — the problem is not the economy, it is stolen money.

questions.prompt: Kidnappers have taken schoolchildren from a school in Kaduna. What should the President do?

options.text: Go to the bush with the security forces and pursue them personally.
Devolve policing to states so local intelligence and accountability improve.
Restructure the entire security architecture and hold service chiefs accountable for outcomes.
Treat insecurity as a symptom of poverty and unemployment — invest in jobs and education as the real security strategy.

questions.prompt: What is the root cause of Nigeria's insecurity?

options.text: Weak leadership and corruption at the top — the President must lead from the front.
A broken federal policing model — states need their own police.
Economic exclusion and poverty — hungry, jobless young men are recruited into violence.
Ethno-religious division — until Nigeria is united, security will remain elusive.

questions.prompt: Should the federal government negotiate with bandits and insurgents?

options.text: Yes — negotiate from a position of strength to secure the release of hostages and reduce violence.
No — pursue them into their hideouts and dismantle their networks.
Only through community-level reconciliation and amnesty, not federal deals.
The question is wrong — the focus should be on preventing recruitment through jobs and education.

questions.prompt: Should the presidency rotate between the North and South in 2027?

options.text: Yes — it is an unwritten rule that has kept Nigeria together, and it must be respected.
No — competence and integrity matter more than where a candidate is from.
Yes, but rotation must be accompanied by performance — rotating power without rotating results is useless.
The whole system needs restructuring — power should devolve to regions and states, making the presidency less powerful.

questions.prompt: What is the single most important constitutional reform Nigeria needs?

options.text: Restructuring — devolve power and resources to states and regions.
An electoral threshold requiring 50%+1 to win the presidency, forcing broad coalitions.
State police and local government autonomy.
Free and compulsory education from primary to university.

questions.prompt: Nigeria's out-of-school children crisis is the worst in the world. What should be done?

options.text: Declare a state of emergency on education and make basic education free and compulsory.
Invest in teacher training and school infrastructure, with measurable performance targets.
Leave it to states — education is a state matter and federal intervention has failed.
Focus on skills and vocational training, not just academic education — the jobs are not there for graduates anyway.
Yes — free and compulsory from primary to university, funded by cutting waste.
No — but student loans should be genuinely accessible and not debt traps.
Yes for STEM and education degrees, no for others — target subsidy where it has the highest return.
The focus should be on primary and secondary education first — free university is a luxury Nigeria cannot afford yet.

questions.prompt: A governor is accused of stealing ₦50 billion. What should happen?

options.text: The President should lead a visible anti-corruption fight and ensure prosecution regardless of party.
The institutions (EFCC, ICPC, courts) should handle it without presidential interference.
The money should be recovered and returned to the state — prosecution is secondary to restitution.
This is why power should devolve — local accountability is more effective than federal anti-corruption theatre.

questions.prompt: How should Nigeria's oil revenue be managed?

options.text: Channel excess revenue above the budget benchmark directly into citizen welfare programmes.
Save it in a sovereign wealth fund for future generations and economic stability.
Remove the subsidy entirely and let the market allocate resources efficiently.
Use it to restore the subsidy and keep fuel prices affordable for ordinary Nigerians.
